title: The 150 DSA problems I'd actually do before a coding interview (Java & Python)
author: Code Notes
summary: Most "interview prep" lists are 500 problems long. Nobody finishes them. Interviewers at most companies test the same ~15 patterns again and again, so a short list that covers every pattern beats a long list that covers the same one ten times. Here's how I'd group a 150-problem plan: Arrays & hashing (20) — two-sum style lookups, counting, prefix sums. Two pointers & sliding window (20) — sorted arrays, longest/shortest substring problems. Stacks & queues (10) — valid brackets, next greater element, monotonic stack. Binary search (10) — not just "find x": search on the answer. Linked lists (10) — reverse, merge, cycle detection. Trees (20) — DFS/BFS, BST checks, lowest common ancestor. Heaps (8) — top-k, merge k lists, running median. Graphs (15) — BFS shortest path, islands, topological sort, union-find. Backtracking (10) — subsets, permutations, N-Queens. Dynamic programming (22) — 1D (climbing stairs, house robber), 2D (grid paths, LCS), knapsack. Greedy & intervals (5) — merge intervals, meeting rooms. How to work through it: Do one pattern at a time. Don't shuffle. Give each problem 25 minutes. Stuck? Read the idea, close it, write the code yourself. Re-solve anything you needed help with 3 days later. I keep the full list, with a lesson for every pattern and an online judge to submit solutions, here (free): Java: https://www.mentornxt.com/learn/java/dsa-sheet?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=wk1 Python: https://www.mentornxt.com/learn/python/dsa-sheet?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=wk1 (Disclosure: I help build MentorNxt.)

title: Turning Coding Practice into Real-Time 1v1 PvP Duels
author: Julius
summary: Check out our official Devpost submission here: https://devpost.com/software/codewatch-wm83fl Inspiration The fastest way to improve as a programmer is through high-stakes competition—whether that is technical interviews, demanding engineering roles, or competitive programming contests. However, all of these share one major flaw: waiting. Weekly contests only happen once a week, major competitions happen monthly or annually, and beginners breaking into the field rarely get daily interview practice. Inspired by the fast-paced matchmaking of Overwatch, we wanted to eliminate the wait time and let developers sharpen their skills on demand. Our Philosophy: Blue vs. Red Great code isn't written in isolation; it's proven through competition. Programming is about thinking faster, adapting smarter, and staying calm under pressure. We built CodeWatch around a core visual and competitive rivalry: • The Blue Character (You): Represents intelligence, precision, creativity, and clean code. Blue embodies the developer who anticipates edge cases and outsmarts the competition. • The Red Demon (Your Opponent): Represents chaos, unexpected challenges, and the constant threat of being outperformed. Red is always lurking, waiting to exploit a bug or pull ahead. Victory comes down to pure skill. Don't just write code—compete with it, outsmart your opponent, and win the duel. What CodeWatch Does CodeWatch brings instant, on-the-spot matchmaking to coding: • 1v1 Coding Duels: Players queue up and immediately face off against another developer in a real-time coding battle. • The Cyber-Range: For developers interested in cybersecurity, the Cyber-Range lets players write defensive code designed to withstand attacks. If your defenses hold, you earn rewards. If another player breaks through your code, they steal your resources. Instead of waiting days or weeks for the next scheduled contest, developers can jump into live matches whenever they want to practice. How We Built It We combined modern web frameworks with real-time code execution tools to handle matchmaking, sessions, and live judging: • Frontend: Built with React and TypeScript for a responsive, game-like user interface. • Backend & Database: Powered by Python (FastAPI) and Node.js. FastAPI handles our core routes, rate limits, and compiling logic while communicating with Node to read submission data. We used SQLModel alongside SQLAlchemy to manage concurrent match sessions, user sessions, and judge sessions, paired with JWT for authentication and database state handling. • Code Execution: Integrated Judge0 and external APIs to serve problem sets and deliver reliable, real-time execution feeds to both players during a match. • Infrastructure & AI Tooling: Deployed on DigitalOcean using Docker. We also leveraged Claude AI and Claude Code throughout the hackathon to rapidly prototype frontend iterations, debug server configurations, and accelerate feature development. Challenges We Ran Into • WSL2 & Judge0 Compatibility: Running Judge0 locally on a Windows machine using WSL2 caused system-level restrictions that blocked execution logic. Moving our testing environment onto a dedicated DigitalOcean server resolved the bottleneck and allowed us to properly test live PvP matches. • Recursive Matchmaking Bugs: Our JavaScript player-finder queue initially suffered from a bug where the matchmaking function recursively called itself twice, hitting execution limits and abruptly dropping players from the queue. Refactoring the queue state fixed the loop and stabilized matchmaking. • Start up failures: With each deployment, there's risk of failure. For instance, deploying our new Agent Prompt feature, a use-minimal-tokens competition, we had to migrate our server to fit its needs. Additionally, the prompt feature didn't work for some commits, which we thankfully fixed by connecting both the local and server's database to the Agent. • Scope: To avoid overengineering out project, the teams decided to place our ideas but note them as "coming soon" (or "incomplete"). For instance, the game modes that are 2v2 or higher are behind this wall. However, this is to show the plans we have for this application after the event. Accomplishments We're Proud Of Getting Version 1 live and watching two players successfully match, write code, and get judged in real time on our DigitalOcean server was a huge milestone. Our team also divided responsibilities cleanly across frontend, backend, and infrastructure, making code integration and debugging much smoother than expected. What We Learned This was our first time building a gamified developer platform. Along the way, we gained hands-on experience with real-time app deployment, Docker containerization, collaborative Git workflows, and managing concurrent session states under pressure. What's Next for CodeWatch During our research, we were surprised to find that an instant-queue, 1v1 PvP coding platform like this didn't really exist yet. Based on the momentum from our initial build, we plan to open-source CodeWatch so developers across software engineering and cybersecurity can contribute new game modes, problem sets, and features. Try it here: https://codewatch.us/

title: Stop being your team's human database: a self-serve answers page in one small file
author: FactQL
summary:
If you have database access, you know the message: "Got a sec? Can you pull a number for me?" Sales wants a number. Support wants a number. Finance wants theirs by five. Each one is small. Together they eat the day, and every one costs you the time it takes to get back into what you were doing. This post builds the smallest thing that removes you from that loop: one page where a colleague types a question and gets an answer they can check without you . What "an answer they can check" means If the page only shows a sentence, people will come back and ask you to confirm it. So every answer needs three parts: The answer in words. The rows it came from. The query that ran , folded away for anyone who wants it. With those three on screen, "is this right?" stops being a question for you. The whole app One Flask file. It serves a page and proxies questions to FactQL , which returns the answer, the rows and the query in one JSON response. You don't need to sign up to try it: without a key, the script borrows FactQL's public sample key, which points at a demo film-rental shop. # pip install flask requests import os , requests from flask import Flask , request , jsonify , render_template_string app = Flask ( __name__ ) FACTQL = "https://api.factql.ai" def api_key ( ) : # Use your own key if you have one; otherwise borrow the public sample key. key = os . environ . get ( "FACTQL_API_KEY" ) if not key : key = requests . get ( f "{FACTQL}/sample" , timeout = 30 ) . json ( ) [ "api_key" ] return key KEY = api_key ( ) PAGE = """ Ask the data

Ask the data

""" @app . get ( "/" ) def home ( ) : return render_template_string ( PAGE ) @app . post ( "/ask" ) def ask ( ) : q = ( request . get_json ( silent = True ) or { } ) . get ( "q" , "" ) . strip ( ) if not q : return jsonify ( error = "Type a question first." ) , 400 r = requests . post ( f "{FACTQL}/query" , headers = { "X-API-Key" : KEY } , json = { "q" : q } , timeout = 120 ) if r . status_code == 429 : return jsonify ( error = f "Too many questions. Try again in {r.headers.get('Retry-After', 'a few')} seconds." ) , 429 r . raise_for_status ( ) a = r . json ( ) # Pass on only what the page shows. return jsonify ( { k : a . get ( k ) for k in ( "result" , "explanation" , "data" , "sql" , "lineage" ) } ) if __name__ == "__main__" : app . run ( port = 5000 ) Run it: pip install flask requests python app.py # open http://localhost:5000 What comes back I asked "Who are our top 5 customers by total spend?". This is the real response from the sample data (trimmed to the fields the page shows): { "result" : "success" , "explanation" : "Your top 5 customers by total payments are Karl Seal (358.12), Tim Cary (344.06), Russell Brinson (324.04), Harry Arce (323.17) and Daisy Bates (322.12)." , "data" : { "columns" : [ "first_name" , "last_name" , "total_spend" ] , "rows" : [ [ "KARL" , "SEAL" , 358.12 ] , [ "TIM" , "CARY" , 344.06 ] , [ "RUSSELL" , "BRINSON" , 324.04 ] , [ "HARRY" , "ARCE" , 323.17 ] , [ "DAISY" , "BATES" , 322.12 ] ] } , "sql" : "SELECT c.first_name, c.last_name, SUM(p.amount) AS total_spend FROM payment p JOIN customer c ON c.customer_id = p.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name ORDER BY total_spend DESC LIMIT 5" } (The raw amounts come back as floats like 358.1200000000005 ; round them when you display money.) The page shows the sentence, draws the rows as a table, and tucks the query under "The query that ran". Four things worth getting right Keep the key on the server. The browser talks to /ask , never to the upstream service. A key in page code can be read by anyone who opens the page. Write values with textContent , not innerHTML . Answers and rows are data. Treat them as text so nothing in a cell can run as markup. Use a read-only database user when you point this at your own database instead of the sample. Handle 429. The sample key allows only a couple of questions a minute per IP, so the proxy passes the wait time on instead of failing silently. Pointing it at your own data Set FACTQL_API_KEY to your own key and the same file works against your data: an uploaded CSV or Excel file, or a PostgreSQL or MySQL database connected with a read-only user. The free plan needs no card. When not to do this If people ask the same five questions every week, a dashboard is the better tool. This page is for the long tail: the questions nobody predicted, which are exactly the ones that land in your DMs. What's the "quick question" you get asked most often?

title: Algorithmic Counter-Pressing: Quantifying Rest-Defense and Transition Vulnerability
author: Football Tale
summary: When analyzing high-possession football systems, public commentary tends to fixate on passing sequences in the attacking third. In elite analytics departments, however, data scientists increasingly focus on the spatial geometry behind the ball: rest-defense . A team's transition vulnerability is determined in the micro-seconds before possession is lost. If an attacking unit loses the ball without a coherent 3-2 or 2-3 defensive structure behind it, the probability of conceding a high-threat transition spike increases exponentially. Modeling Transition Packing Rates To quantify counter-pressing efficacy, tracking algorithms measure packing rates and recovery radius density : Pitch Partitioning: Dividing the pitch into Voronoi cells dynamically updated at 25 fps. Centroid Contraction: Measuring the velocity at which the defensive midfield pivot collapses toward the ball carrier within 2.5 seconds of a turnover. Transition Lockdown: Calculating whether the ball carrier has at least two passing lanes obstructed by defensive cones. # Conceptual transition density metric def calculate_transition_density ( defenders , turnover_pos , radius = 12.0 ) : """Calculates defensive containment density within immediate recovery radius (meters).""" in_radius = [ d for d in defenders if euclidean_distance ( d . pos , turnover_pos ) <= radius ] return len ( in_radius ) / ( math . pi * ( radius ** 2 ) ) When teams execute counter-pressing successfully, they don't just win tackles—they compress the ball-carrier's decision window to under 0.8 seconds, forcing errant clearances that can be recycled into a secondary wave of attack. We break down the structural blueprints of elite pressing systems and rest-defense architectures in our complete counter-pressing masterclass on Football Tale. title: Mexico City stopped changing its clocks in 2022. Your overlap spreadsheet probably didn't notice
author: Bromena
summary: If you work with engineers in Mexico City and you planned your meetings before late 2022, your mental model of the overlap is probably wrong for half the year. Mexico City dropped daylight saving time. It has been on Zona Centro, UTC-6, all year since October 30, 2022, under the Ley de los Husos Horarios published in the DOF. US cities still change their clocks twice a year. So the shared hours now move only when the US moves. Computing it instead of remembering it Python's zoneinfo reads the IANA time zone database, which already has the 2022 change. A 9-to-6 workday on both sides: from datetime import datetime , date , time , timedelta from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo def workday ( d , tz , start = 9 , end = 18 ) : z = ZoneInfo ( tz ) return datetime . combine ( d , time ( start ) , z ) , datetime . combine ( d , time ( end ) , z ) def overlap_hours ( d , tz ) : a0 , a1 = workday ( d , "America/Mexico_City" ) b0 , b1 = workday ( d , tz ) return max ( timedelta ( 0 ) , min ( a1 , b1 ) - max ( a0 , b0 ) ) . total_seconds ( ) / 3600 for city , tz in [ ( "New York" , "America/New_York" ) , ( "Chicago" , "America/Chicago" ) , ( "Denver" , "America/Denver" ) , ( "Los Angeles" , "America/Los_Angeles" ) ] : print ( city , overlap_hours ( date ( 2027 , 1 , 15 ) , tz ) , overlap_hours ( date ( 2027 , 7 , 15 ) , tz ) ) US city US winter (standard) US summer (daylight) New York, Toronto 8 h 7 h Chicago 9 h 8 h Denver 8 h 9 h Los Angeles, San Francisco 7 h 8 h The part that surprises people Chicago loses an hour in summer. Before 2022 Mexico City and Chicago moved together and always matched. Now they match only in US winter. Denver and the West Coast gain an hour in summer. When the US springs forward, Mountain and Pacific time move closer to UTC-6. New York drops to 7 hours from mid-March. In 2022, a July date gave New York 8 shared hours with Mexico City. In July 2027 it's 7. In 2027 the switch dates for US teams are March 14 and November 7. Those are the two days a recurring "10 AM Mexico" standup lands at a different US time. Takeaways Store meeting times with an IANA zone ( America/Mexico_City ), never a fixed offset or "CST". Recompute overlap per date instead of keeping one number in a doc. If a team spans several US zones, the best shared window changes in March and November. Revisit it then. We publish the per-city table and how we plan shared hours for nearshore teams at https://bromena.com/ — Bromena team

title: Exploring Mobile Game Performance Optimization and User Engagement Trends
author: Nathan Ertel
summary: Introduction Modern mobile app development and lightweight interactive gaming experiences have evolved rapidly over the past few years. Developers are constantly looking for ways to balance seamless UI/UX design, low battery consumption, and engaging user mechanics on web and mobile platforms. In this article, we will analyze the core architecture behind lightweight mobile gaming interfaces and how performance benchmarks impact user retention. Key Factors in Mobile Game Performance When building or reviewing interactive mobile applications, several technical constraints must be addressed: Rendering Efficiency: Minimizing DOM reflows and utilizing hardware-accelerated CSS or WebGL components. Asset Optimization: Compression of sprites, textures, and scripts to ensure fast load times across low-end and high-end devices. State Management: Keeping real-time scorecards and user progress synced without overloading local storage or backend servers. Case Study & Interactive Workflows To understand how these concepts are applied in real-world scenarios, developers often look at deployed web-app hybrid games. For instance, analyzing practical implementations like the Jan111 Game overview on OnlineApp gives a clear perspective on how lightweight entertainment apps structure their user flows and interface elements for optimal speed. Conclusion Optimizing mobile applications and interactive tools requires a continuous focus on performance tuning and clean code architecture. By keeping bundle sizes small and user navigation intuitive, developers can deliver exceptional digital experiences across all devices.

title: Prototype First: Test Your Idea in 30 Minutes Before You Spend Six Months Building It
author: Davis George
summary: Every developer knows the expensive question: is this idea worth six months of my life? For most of us, the honest answer used to be "I don't know until I build it" — and building it was the six months. That equation is changing. AI coding agents can now turn a rough idea into a clickable, working prototype in well under an hour. The prototype won't be the product. But it can answer the question that matters most: should I build this at all? That shift — from "build to find out" to "prototype to decide" — is quietly becoming the most valuable skill in AI-assisted development. Here's how to use it well. The prototype is a question, not a product A prototype has one job: to make the idea concrete enough to judge. It needs to answer three questions: Does the core interaction feel right? Can a user do the one thing the app exists for, end to end? Is the hard part actually hard? Every idea has one risky piece — a tricky integration, a workflow nobody has nailed, a performance constraint. The prototype should touch that piece first. Would anyone care? Show it to five real people. Watch where they hesitate. Their confusion is data. Notice what is not on that list: clean code, a design system, authentication, billing, tests, deployment pipelines. A prototype that has all of those is not a prototype — it's a product with a deadline you didn't need. The 30-minute loop Here is the loop I use when an idea is worth testing but not yet worth committing to: 1. Write the one-paragraph brief first Before touching any agent, write a short brief in plain language: Who is it for? What is the single thing they do with it? What does "working" look like in a demo? Keep it under 150 words. If you can't describe the idea in a paragraph, the agent can't build it either — and that confusion is itself useful information. 2. Give the agent a throwaway job Tell the agent explicitly that this is disposable: use the simplest stack, hardcode the data, skip auth, skip tests. A typical prompt looks like this: Build a throwaway prototype, not production code. Stack: a single-page app, no auth, no database — hardcode sample data. Goal: let a user paste a URL and see a summary card in under 2 seconds. Stop when the core flow works in the browser. Do not add features. The words "throwaway" and "stop when" matter. Without them, agents keep polishing — adding settings pages, refactoring, gold-plating — and your 30-minute test becomes a 3-hour project. 3. Run agents in parallel, not in sequence One of the biggest practical wins is running several agents at once, each on a different angle of the same idea: one builds the main flow, one tries a different UI approach, one attacks the risky integration. You compare the results and keep the best. A simple way to organise it: Terminal 1: agent A — build the core flow (input → output) Terminal 2: agent B — build an alternative UI for the same flow Terminal 3: agent C — spike the risky part (the API call, the parser, the export) Three prototypes in 30 minutes tell you far more than one polished prototype in three hours, because the comparison itself is information: which approach felt natural, which one broke, which one a user understood without explanation. 4. Demo it to a human within the hour A prototype sitting on your laptop has answered nothing. Show it to someone — a friend, a colleague, a user from the target audience — and watch them use it without guidance. The moments they pause, misclick, or ask "what does this do?" are the findings. Write them down verbatim; your memory will smooth them over by tomorrow. 5. Decide, then delete or commit After the demo, make a binary call: Kill it. The idea doesn't survive contact with a user. You spent 30 minutes, not six months. That's a win. Commit to it. The core works and someone wants it. Now — and only now — throw the prototype away and start the real build with a proper plan, because prototype code is optimised for speed, not survival. The most common failure mode is the middle path: keeping the prototype and slowly turning it into the product. Prototype code is full of shortcuts that become permanent bugs. If the idea is worth building, it is worth rebuilding properly. What a prototype cannot tell you Being honest about the limits is what makes this workflow trustworthy rather than hype: It can't validate the boring 80%. Auth, payments, error handling, scale, maintenance — the prototype skips all of it, and that is where most products actually live or die. It can't tell you if the code is good. Agents write plausible-looking code fast, and plausible is not the same as correct. The prototype proves the idea can work, not that the code is safe. Review anything you keep. It can't replace your judgement. If the prototype is impressive but you don't understand how it works, you don't own it — you're renting it. The demo that matters most is the one where you can explain every part of what you just built. That last point is also the answer to the most common criticism of this style of working: that it produces developers who can't code. The skill hasn't disappeared; it has moved. It used to be writing every line. Now it's knowing what to ask for, recognising when the output is wrong, and understanding the system well enough to fix it. Developers who build on top of their own experience — their own libraries, their own hard-won knowledge of the domain — get far more out of agents than developers who start from zero, because they know what "good" looks like. The habit that compounds Prototype-first is not a tool choice. It's a habit: every idea gets a cheap test before it gets an expensive commitment. After a few months of it, you build a second skill on top — a sense for which ideas die in the prototype stage and which ones survive. That instinct is worth more than any single tool, because it protects the one resource you can't get back: the six months you would have spent on the wrong thing. So the next time an idea excites you, resist the urge to start building it properly. Build it badly, quickly, in parallel — and let the prototype tell you whether it deserves the real thing. — Written by Davis George · zhuan.xyz

title: Why a canvas re-encode can make a JPEG bigger
author: LighterPics
summary: Disclosure: This report on the image-processing tests run by the LighterPics project was written with AI assistance. Exporting an existing JPEG through a canvas does not guarantee a smaller file. At quality 0.92 , five of 25 test photos grew in Chromium, 10 in Firefox and 11 in WebKit. Engine Photos larger than the input Median output size, as a percentage of input size Chromium 145.0.7632.6 5 of 25 60% Firefox 146.0.1 10 of 25 84% WebKit 26.0 11 of 25 80% All three ran the same photos at the same requested quality. For every photo, the Firefox and WebKit JPEGs were larger than the Chromium JPEG. The quality argument alone was not enough to predict the output size across engines. What changes when a JPEG is re-encoded A canvas export starts from decoded pixels and creates a new file. Its size depends on the output format, encoder settings and image content. The API does not promise to keep it below the input byte count. The converter used createImageBitmap() followed by a canvas export. Its quality settings were passed to toBlob() or the equivalent worker export; PNG does not use that argument. [1] Higher quality often meant a larger file Chromium ran the wider quality sweep. Here are the results for the 25 JPEG photos: Output setting Photos that grew Median size relative to input Range JPEG 1.0 23 of 25 197% 91% to 586% JPEG 0.92 5 of 25 60% 20% to 138% JPEG 0.80 2 of 25 39% 8% to 106% WebP 1.0 25 of 25 250% 141% to 813% WebP 0.92 3 of 25 50% 10% to 152% PNG 25 of 25 483% 224% to 1,267% At JPEG 0.70, no photo grew and the median output size was 26% of the input. No photo grew at any of the lower tested JPEG quality values either. At JPEG quality 1.0, the median output was nearly twice the input size. That setting requests the highest quality, but it still re-encodes the decoded image and cannot recover detail lost in the original JPEG. The recorded median PSNR, a measure of pixel error against the decoded input, was 56.88 dB at 1.0, 43.33 dB at 0.92 and 40.29 dB at 0.80. These were objective measurements, not a visual preference test. WebP at 1.0 took a different path in this Chromium build: all 25 files contained the lossless VP8L bitstream. At 0.92, they contained lossy VP8 . The WebP container specification distinguishes these two formats. [2] Firefox also produced three larger files out of 25 at WebP 0.92, with a median size of 50% of the input. WebKit produced no accepted WebP output. PNG made every photo larger in all three engines; the Firefox and WebKit medians were 383% and 421%, respectively. The five photos that grew at JPEG 0.92 in Chromium also grew in Firefox and WebKit. Four were night shots and one was a portrait. They were among the inputs with the fewest bytes per pixel, but that alone did not explain the result: the lowest-bytes-per-pixel photo shrank in Chromium. The tests did not record encoder libraries or chroma subsampling, so they do not identify the cause of the engine differences. A size target did not guarantee a smaller file The compressor searched for an output that fit a requested byte budget. Across 1,407 Chromium runs that produced a file, it returned 177 files larger than their inputs. Every one had a target at or above the input size. Target relative to input size Runs with an output Output larger than input Target met Target missed Below input size 1,038 0 773 265 At or above input size 369 177 369 0 A re-encoded file can fit the requested budget while still exceeding the original size. In JPEG mode, the compressor first tries quality 0.92. If that output fits, it returns it; otherwise it searches lower qualities and, when allowed, reduces the pixel dimensions. The WebP and MozJPEG traces also started at 0.92 for the runs that produced larger files. Of the 177 larger outputs, 159 came from the first encode at 0.92. The other 18 came from searches that settled between 0.75 and 0.91. All met the target, but none reduced the input byte count. Reducing pixel dimensions helped when the target was below the input size: the compressor met the target in 543 of 549 runs with resizing allowed, compared with 230 of 489 without it. Successful runs in that group reached a median of 98.4% of the target. When the target was missed, the tool returned its smallest attempt; those outputs still did not exceed the input size in this test set. For the single cross-engine compressor setting, JPEG with a 200 KB target and resizing allowed, all 25 photos came in under the target in every engine. That result does not extend to all targets or settings. If a tool must never increase file size, it needs a separate comparison against the input byte count. Checking only the requested target is insufficient. The starting format also mattered Converting PNG to JPEG was not a reliable way to shrink the generated screenshots and graphics. At JPEG 0.92 in Chromium, four of five screenshots grew, with a median output size of 122% of the input. Three of five graphics grew, with a median of 110%. A separate test first converted each of the 25 photos to WebP at 0.80. Those WebPs were a median of 23% of the original JPEG size. Converting them again made every file larger than its intermediate WebP: Conversion from WebP 0.80 Median size relative to WebP Range JPEG 0.92 2.31× 1.59× to 3.37× JPEG 0.80 1.49× 1.02× to 1.88× PNG 18.41× 9.72× to 25.87× These ratios use the intermediate WebP as the reference file. Reproduce one example This short example uses one of the photos that grew at JPEG 0.92. Open about:blank in a desktop browser and paste it into the DevTools console. The Wikimedia file server allows the cross-origin request. ( async ( ) => { const src = await ( await fetch ( "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0f/Star_night_%28Unsplash%29.jpg" ) ) . blob ( ) ; const bitmap = await createImageBitmap ( src , { imageOrientation : "from-image" } ) ; const canvas = document . createElement ( "canvas" ) ; canvas . width = bitmap . width ; canvas . height = bitmap . height ; canvas . getContext ( "2d" ) . drawImage ( bitmap , 0 , 0 ) ; for ( const [ type , quality ] of [ [ "image/jpeg" , 1 ] , [ "image/jpeg" , 0.92 ] , [ "image/jpeg" , 0.8 ] , [ "image/png" ] ] ) { const out = await new Promise ( resolve => canvas . toBlob ( resolve , type , quality ) ) ; console . log ( type , quality ?? "" , out . type , out . size , ( 100 * out . size / src . size ) . toFixed ( 0 ) + "% of the original" ) ; } } ) ( ) ; The input is 878,879 bytes. The recorded outputs were: Output Chromium output, in bytes JPEG 1.0 4,145,012 JPEG 0.92 1,140,171 JPEG 0.80 798,492 PNG 8,707,460 At JPEG 0.92, Firefox produced 1,557,092 bytes and WebKit 1,690,770 bytes. title: Sitemaps, Canonicals & OG Images From Your Nuxt Backend
author: Muhammad Ali Mughal
summary: Most SEO problems I inherit on Nuxt projects are not content problems. They are plumbing problems: a sitemap generated once at build time and never updated, canonical tags that keep every ?utm_ and ?sort= variant alive, and Open Graph images that return an HTML 404 page instead of a PNG. If your catalog, listings or case studies live in a database, those three outputs should come from the same database, at request time, with sane caching. I run Loop Origin , a software studio, and as a Principal Software Engineer I have spent nine years shipping Laravel, Vue and Nuxt applications. I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every command, header and code sample myself. This guide shows how I generate sitemaps, canonicals and OG images from the backend, with real HTTP output, a comparison of approaches and the failure modes I see in production. How should a Nuxt app generate sitemaps, canonicals and OG images? Direct answer: Generate all three from your backend data at request time. Serve sitemap.xml from a Nitro server route backed by your API, set one normalised canonical URL per page with useHead , and render OG images through a cached image endpoint that returns image/png . Cache aggressively and invalidate when content changes. Why build-time SEO files break on dynamic sites A static sitemap.xml is fine for a ten-page brochure site. It breaks the moment content changes without a deploy: A new product, listing or blog post goes live, but crawlers do not see it in the sitemap until the next build. A deleted page stays in the sitemap and returns 404, which wastes crawl budget and looks sloppy in Search Console. lastmod values become the build date for every URL, which tells crawlers nothing useful. The same is true of OG images rendered by a designer once per template. They go stale when the title changes, and nobody notices until a sales lead shares a link in Slack and the preview shows last year's headline. If you are still deciding how much of the app to server-render in the first place, my earlier comparison of Nuxt 3 rendering modes for B2B SaaS covers that trade-off. Everything below assumes the public pages are SSR or hybrid. What good looks like in real responses Before writing code, I check what mature sites return. Here is curl output from Nov 15, 2026. GitHub renders a dynamic OG image per repository and caches it hard: $ curl -sI "https://opengraph.githubassets.com/932c33d9.../laravel/framework" \ | grep -iE "^HTTP|content-type|cache-control|content-length" HTTP/2 200 cache-control: public, max-age=21600, immutable content-type: image/png content-length: 48567 Nuxt's own documentation site serves a generated sitemap with the right content type: $ curl -sI https://nuxt.com/sitemap.xml | grep -iE "^HTTP|content-type" HTTP/2 200 content-type: text/xml ; charset = UTF-8 $ curl -s https://nuxt.com/sitemap.xml | grep -o "<loc>" | wc -l 883 Three things to copy: a real 200 , an image or XML content type, and an explicit cache policy. The failure I find most often in audits is the opposite: an og:image URL that returns HTTP 404 with content-type: text/html , so every social share silently falls back to no image. Approaches compared Approach Fresh after content change Scales past 50,000 URLs Ops effort Best fit Static files in public/ Only on redeploy Manual splitting Very low Brochure sites Build-time generation ( nuxi generate ) Only on rebuild Yes, with index Low Docs, small blogs Nuxt SEO modules with an API source Yes, with cache TTL Yes, built-in chunking Low to medium Most Nuxt apps Custom Nitro server routes Yes, event-driven Yes, you write the index Medium Catalogs, marketplaces, multi-tenant Laravel backend generates, Nuxt proxies Yes Yes Medium Teams with backend-owned SEO data I default to custom Nitro routes when the data model is unusual (multi-tenant, per-locale, per-vendor) and to a module when the site is standard. The sitemap protocol limits each file to 50,000 URLs and 50 MB uncompressed, so anything larger needs a sitemap index either way. Sitemap from the database The backend exposes a lean, paginated endpoint. In Laravel: // routes/api.php Route :: get ( '/seo/urls' , function ( Request $request ) { $page = max ( 1 , ( int ) $request -> query ( 'page' , 1 ) ) ; return Product :: query ( ) -> where ( 'status' , 'published' ) -> select ( [ 'slug' , 'updated_at' ] ) -> orderBy ( 'id' ) -> forPage ( $page , 45000 ) -> get ( ) -> map ( fn ( $p ) => [ 'loc' => "/products/{$p->slug}" , 'lastmod' => $p -> updated_at -> toDateString ( ) ] ) ; } ) -> middleware ( 'cache.headers:public;max_age=900' ) ; Nuxt serves the XML from a Nitro route with a cache in front: // server/routes/sitemap/[page].xml.ts export default defineCachedEventHandler ( async ( event ) => { const page = Number ( getRouterParam ( event , 'page' ) ? . replace ( '.xml' , '' ) || 1 ) const urls = await $fetch < { loc : string ; lastmod : string } [ ] > ( `${useRuntimeConfig().apiBase}/seo/urls` , { query : { page } } ) const base = 'https://www.yourstore.com' const body = urls . map ( u => `<url><loc>${base}${u.loc}</loc><lastmod>${u.lastmod}</lastmod></url>` ) . join ( '' ) setHeader ( event , 'content-type' , 'application/xml; charset=utf-8' ) return `<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>` + `<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">${body}</urlset>` } , { maxAge : 900 , swr : true , getKey : e => getRouterParam ( e , 'page' ) || '1' } ) A sitemap.xml index route lists /sitemap/1.xml , /sitemap/2.xml and so on. Keep lastmod honest: use the content's real update time, not now() . Escape & in any URL that carries query strings. And make sure every URL in the sitemap is the canonical version, returns 200 and is indexable. One canonical per page Canonicals go wrong in three predictable ways: tracking parameters, sort and filter parameters, and trailing-slash or case variants. I normalise in one composable: // composables/useCanonical.ts const KEEP = new Set ( [ 'page' ] ) // params that create a distinct page export function useCanonical ( ) { const route = useRoute ( ) const base = 'https://www.yourstore.com' const params = Object . entries ( route . query ) . filter ( ( [ k ] ) => KEEP . has ( k ) ) . sort ( ( [ a ] , [ b ] ) => a . localeCompare ( b ) ) const qs = new URLSearchParams ( params as [ string , string ] [ ] ) . toString ( ) const path = route . path . toLowerCase ( ) . replace ( / \ /+ $ / , '' ) || '/' const href = `${base}${path}${qs ? ` ? ${qs} ` : ''}` useHead ( { link : [ { rel : 'canonical' , href } ] } ) useSeoMeta ( { ogUrl : href } ) return href } Rules I agree with the content team up front: utm_* , gclid , sort and view toggles never appear in a canonical; real pagination does; filtered category pages are canonical only when we intend them to rank. When a site moves or a URL scheme changes, the canonical rules and the redirect map have to change together, which I covered in the replatforming redirect map playbook . Image: AI-generated. OG images as a cached endpoint A link preview needs an absolute og:image URL that returns a real image, ideally 1200×630. I render it on the server from the page's title and a brand template, then cache it at the CDN: // server/routes/og/[slug].png.ts import { renderOgPng } from '~/server/utils/og' // wraps satori + resvg export default defineCachedEventHandler ( async ( event ) => { const slug = getRouterParam ( event , 'slug' ) ! . replace ( '.png' , '' ) const product = await $fetch < { name : string ; price : string } > ( `${useRuntimeConfig().apiBase}/products/${slug}/og` ) . catch ( ( ) => null ) if ( ! product ) { return sendRedirect ( event , '/og/default.png' , 302 ) // never a HTML 404 } setHeader ( event , 'content-type' , 'image/png' ) setHeader ( event , 'cache-control' , 'public, max-age=86400, stale-while-revalidate=604800' ) return renderOgPng ( { title : product . name , subtitle : product . price } ) } , { maxAge : 86400 , getKey : e => getRouterParam ( e , 'slug' ) ! } ) On the page: useSeoMeta({ ogImage: `https://www.yourstore.com/og/${slug}.png`, twitterCard: 'summary_large_image' }) . Add a version or updated_at hash to the URL ( /og/${slug}.png?v=1731650000 ) so a title change produces a fresh image instead of a cached old one. Social platforms cache previews on their side too, so the version parameter is what makes a re-share pick up the new image. Cost and effort For a typical catalog of 10,000–100,000 URLs, the work is small compared to the traffic it protects. These are my planning estimates for a team that already runs Nuxt and Laravel, not quotes: Item Effort estimate Ongoing cost driver Paginated SEO URL endpoint + sitemap index 1–2 days Database reads, cached 15 min Canonical composable + rules doc 1 day Review when routes change OG image endpoint with template 2–3 days CPU per render, cached 24 h CI checks for status, content type, canonical 1 day None Launch checklist [ ] curl -sI /sitemap.xml returns 200 and an XML content type; every child sitemap stays under 50,000 URLs. [ ] Every sitemap URL returns 200 , is indexable and matches its own canonical. [ ] lastmod reflects real content updates. [ ] robots.txt lists the sitemap index URL. [ ] Canonicals are absolute, lowercase, without tracking or sort parameters. [ ] og:image URLs are absolute, return image/png or image/jpeg , and never text/html . [ ] Missing content falls back to a default OG image, not an error page. [ ] Cache headers are explicit and content updates purge or version the cached files. [ ] A CI job spot-checks 20 random URLs for all of the above. Failure modes I see in production Sitemap lists non-canonical URLs. Search Console reports "Duplicate, Google chose different canonical than user" by the thousand. Staging leaks. The sitemap is built from an environment variable that still points at staging. on production. OG endpoint behind auth or bot protection. Social crawlers get a challenge page and show no preview. Uncached image rendering. A viral share triggers thousands of renders and the API slows down for real users. Canonical set client-side only. In SPA mode the canonical is missing from the initial HTML that crawlers fetch. FAQ Should I use a Nuxt SEO module or write my own routes? Use a module when your site is a standard content or catalog site; it handles chunking, indexes and defaults well. Write custom Nitro routes when you have multi-tenant domains, per-vendor catalogs or unusual URL rules the module cannot express cleanly. How often should a dynamic sitemap refresh? Cache it for 10–60 minutes with stale-while-revalidate, and purge on publish if your CDN supports it. Crawlers do not need second-by-second freshness, and the cache protects your database during crawl spikes. Do filtered category pages need their own canonical? Only if you want them to rank as distinct pages with unique content and demand. Otherwise point them to the unfiltered category canonical. Decide per filter with your SEO lead and encode the rule in one place. What size should OG images be? 1200×630 pixels is the widely supported size for large link previews. Keep the file small, use PNG or JPEG, keep important text away from the edges, and always return an absolute HTTPS URL. Why does my link preview still show the old image? Social platforms cache previews independently of your CDN. Add a version parameter based on the content's update time to the og:image URL, then use each platform's debugging tool to re-scrape the page. Can the Laravel backend generate the sitemap instead of Nuxt? Yes. Many teams let Laravel write the XML and have Nuxt proxy or redirect /sitemap.xml to it. Keep a single source of URL rules either way, so the sitemap and canonical logic cannot drift apart. Conclusion Sitemaps, canonicals and OG images are three views of the same data: which pages exist, which URL is the real one and how each page looks when shared. Generate them from the backend at request time, cache them deliberately and test them in CI, and the SEO layer stops being something you fix after every release. title: Open Redirects: Find and Fix Them Before Phishers Do
author: Muhammad Ali Mughal
summary: An open redirect is the bug security teams love to mark "low" and phishers love to use. Your login page takes a next parameter, sends the user wherever it says, and suddenly a link that starts with your real, trusted domain lands a victim on a credential-harvesting page. The fix is not a smarter regex. It is a small allowlist function, written once and used by every redirect in the app. I build PixelValut , a set of free browser-side security tools. I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every command, output and claim myself. Below are real responses from a tiny test server I ran on Nov 15, 2026, the bypass payloads that defeat naive checks, and the validation pattern I ship instead. What is an open redirect and how do you fix it? Direct answer: An open redirect is an endpoint that forwards users to any URL supplied in a parameter, letting attackers borrow your domain's trust for phishing or OAuth token theft. Fix it by accepting only same-origin relative paths or an explicit allowlist of exact hostnames, parsed with a real URL parser, and falling back to a safe default. Why a "low severity" bug matters On its own, an open redirect does not leak data from your server. The damage comes from what it enables: Phishing with a real domain. A link like https://app.yourco.com/login?next=https://yourco-support.example/reset passes the "check the domain before you click" advice that every security awareness course teaches. Email filters that score links by domain reputation see your domain first. OAuth and SSO token theft. If an identity provider allows a redirect URI on your domain, and that page forwards anywhere, an attacker can chain the two. The authorization code or token in the URL fragment can follow the browser to the attacker's host. Referrer and token leaks. Password-reset or magic-link pages that redirect onward can leak the token in the URL to the next site, which is why I pair this fix with a strict Referrer-Policy for sensitive URLs . Allowlist bypasses in other systems. SSRF filters, webhook validators and CSP rules that trust your domain can be steered to an external host through your redirect. So the real question is not "can this redirect hurt us" but "what else trusts our domain". A real test: vulnerable vs fixed To show the behaviour without touching anyone's production system, I ran a 30-line Python server locally with two endpoints. /login/vuln copies next straight into the Location header. /login/safe runs it through a validator. Here are the actual responses: vuln next=/settings -> Location: /settings vuln next=https://evil.example/login -> Location: https://evil.example/login vuln next=//evil.example -> Location: //evil.example vuln next=/%5Cevil.example -> Location: /\evil.example vuln next=https:evil.example -> Location: https:evil.example vuln next=https://app.example.test.evil.example/ -> Location: https://app.example.test.evil.example/ safe next=/settings -> Location: /settings safe next=https://evil.example/login -> Location: /dashboard safe next=//evil.example -> Location: /dashboard safe next=/%5Cevil.example -> Location: /dashboard safe next=https:evil.example -> Location: /dashboard safe next=https://app.example.test/billing -> Location: https://app.example.test/billing safe next=https://app.example.test.evil.example/ -> Location: /dashboard Each of those vulnerable lines is a classic bypass: //evil.example is a protocol-relative URL . It starts with a slash, so a check like startsWith("/") passes it, and the browser treats it as https://evil.example . /\evil.example relies on browsers normalising a backslash to a forward slash in the authority part, which turns it into //evil.example . https:evil.example has a scheme but no slashes. Some parsers call it a relative path; browsers often resolve it to the external host. app.example.test.evil.example defeats a contains("app.example.test") or startsWith hostname check, because the attacker owns evil.example and every name under it. Naive checks vs a parsed allowlist Check Example code Stops https://evil.example Stops //evil.example Stops /\evil.example Stops look-alike subdomain No validation redirect($next) No No No No Starts with / str_starts_with($next, '/') Yes No No Yes Substring match str_contains($next, 'yourco.com') Yes No No No Regex on host /^https:\/\/.*yourco\.com/ Yes Often no Often no No Parsed URL + exact host allowlist parse, compare host to a set Yes Yes Yes Yes Server-side redirect IDs ?next=billing mapped to a route Yes Yes Yes Yes The last two rows are the only ones I trust. The ID approach is the strongest when the list of destinations is small, such as "back to billing" or "back to the order". The validation pattern I ship The rules, in order: Reject empty values, anything over a sane length, control characters and backslashes. Allow a relative path only if it starts with a single / and not // . Allow an absolute URL only if it parses, uses https , and its hostname is an exact member of an allowlist. Otherwise, redirect to a fixed default page. Never echo the input back in an error. Here it is in Laravel, where most of my login and checkout flows live: // app/Support/SafeRedirect.php final class SafeRedirect { private const ALLOWED_HOSTS = [ 'app.yourco.com' , 'billing.yourco.com' ] ; public static function target ( ? string $next , string $fallback = '/dashboard' ) : string { if ( $next === null || $next === '' || strlen ( $next ) > 2048 ) return $fallback ; if ( preg_match ( '/[\x00-\x1F\\\\]/' , $next ) ) return $fallback ; if ( str_starts_with ( $next , '/' ) && ! str_starts_with ( $next , '//' ) ) { return $next ; // same-origin path } $parts = parse_url ( $next ) ; if ( ( $parts [ 'scheme' ] ?? null ) === 'https' && in_array ( strtolower ( $parts [ 'host' ] ?? '' ) , self :: ALLOWED_HOSTS , true ) && ! isset ( $parts [ 'user' ] ) ) { // blocks https://app.yourco.com@evil.example return $next ; } return $fallback ; } } // In a controller return redirect ( ) -> to ( SafeRedirect :: target ( $request -> query ( 'next' ) ) ) ; And the same idea in Node, using the WHATWG URL parser that browsers also follow: const ALLOWED = new Set ( [ 'app.yourco.com' , 'billing.yourco.com' ] ) ; export function safeTarget ( next , fallback = '/dashboard' ) { if ( ! next || next . length > 2048 || / [ \ x00 - \ x1f \\ ] / . test ( next ) ) return fallback ; if ( next . startsWith ( '/' ) && ! next . startsWith ( '//' ) ) return next ; try { const u = new URL ( next ) ; if ( u . protocol === 'https:' && ALLOWED . has ( u . hostname ) && ! u . username ) return u . href ; } catch { /* not a valid absolute URL */ } return fallback ; } Two details worth calling out. Checking for a user part blocks https://app.yourco.com@evil.example , where everything before @ is a username and the real host is evil.example . And comparing the parsed hostname to an exact set avoids every substring and suffix trick in one move. Image: AI-generated. Where open redirects hide Login next parameters are the famous one, but in audits I find them in quieter places: Logout endpoints with ?return_to= . Language and currency switchers that send you "back where you were" using the Referer header or a back parameter. Email click-tracking links like /t/click?u= . OAuth redirect_uri registrations that use wildcards or prefix matching instead of exact strings. JavaScript redirects: location.href = params.get('url') . These never show up as a 3xx in server logs. If the value can be javascript:alert(1) , it is also a DOM XSS. Framework helpers such as redirect()->back() that trust a forged Referer when there is no session history. How to test your own site From a terminal, curl shows exactly what the server sends without following it: for p in "https://evil.example" "//evil.example" "/%5Cevil.example" "https:evil.example" ; do printf '%-24s ' "$p" curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{redirect_url}\n' "https://app.yourco.com/login?next=$p" done Any response whose redirect points at evil.example is a finding. For JavaScript redirects, open the URL in a private window with DevTools open and watch where the page goes. In the browser, paste the full test URL into the Redirect Chain Checker to see every hop, status code and final destination. It is useful for marketing links too, where a chain of three tracking redirects can end somewhere nobody expected. Only test domains you own or have written permission to test. Rollout checklist [ ] Search the codebase for redirect( , Location: , location.href , window.open and return_to / next / url / continue parameters. [ ] Route every one through a single helper like SafeRedirect::target() . [ ] Replace free-form destinations with route names or IDs wherever the list is short. [ ] Register OAuth redirect URIs as exact strings; remove wildcards. [ ] Add unit tests for //host , /\host , https:host , user@host and look-alike subdomains. [ ] Set Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin (or stricter on token pages). [ ] Mark session cookies Secure , HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax , as covered in auditing cookie security flags , so a redirect cannot become a session leak. [ ] Re-run the curl loop in CI against staging after every auth change. Failure modes I keep seeing Validating, then decoding. The check runs on the raw value, then the framework URL-decodes it again before redirecting. Validate the exact string you will put in Location . Allowlisting the apex with a suffix match. endsWith('yourco.com') also matches evilyourco.com . Compare exact hosts, or check host === 'yourco.com' || host.endsWith('.yourco.com') only if you control every subdomain. Fixing the login page only. Logout, language switchers and email trackers keep the bug alive. Interstitials as the only fix. A "you are leaving this site" page helps for user-generated links, but it does not fix OAuth chains, where no human sees the hop. FAQ Is an open redirect a real vulnerability or just a bug? It is a real vulnerability with context-dependent severity. Alone it enables convincing phishing. Combined with OAuth, SSO or SSRF allowlists that trust your domain, it can lead to token theft or internal requests, which is why I fix every one I find. Can I just block URLs that start with http? No. Protocol-relative values like //evil.example , backslash variants and https:evil.example all skip that check. Parse the URL and compare the hostname to an exact allowlist, or accept only paths that start with one slash. Does a "you are leaving this site" warning page fix it? It reduces phishing risk for human clicks on user-submitted links, but it does not protect OAuth or SSO flows where the redirect happens automatically. Validate destinations first; use an interstitial only for genuinely external user content. How do open redirects affect OAuth? If a provider allows a redirect URI on your domain and that page forwards to any URL, an attacker can route the authorization response through it. Register exact redirect URIs, use PKCE, and make sure the callback page never forwards to untrusted destinations. Are JavaScript redirects safer than server redirects? No. location.href = param has the same open-redirect risk and adds DOM XSS if the value can be a javascript: URL. Apply the same validator in the browser, and only allow https: or same-origin paths. Will fixing open redirects hurt marketing tracking links? Not if you design for it. Keep tracking links pointing to an allowlist of your own domains and approved partners, or store destinations server-side behind an ID. You keep click analytics without letting anyone forward traffic anywhere. Conclusion Every open redirect I have fixed came down to one missing function. Parse the destination, allow same-origin paths and exact hostnames, default to a safe page, and use that helper everywhere your app sends a user onward. Then test the classic bypasses in CI so the bug does not come back with the next login refactor. If you are tightening transport security at the same time, my notes on a safe HSTS preload rollout cover the next layer. title: AI Search Citation Tracking: A 16-Case Evidence Ledger for SEO Teams
author: isabelle dubuis
summary: AI Search Citation Tracking: A 16-Case Evidence Ledger for SEO Teams Decision first: measure four different outcomes separately: a page was eligible to be retrieved, it appeared in a generative answer, the answer linked to that exact page, and a real visit or business outcome followed. One dashboard cannot prove all four. Start with Google’s Search Console generative AI report for the impressions and pages it documents; use a prompt log and citation review for exact answer evidence; use analytics or CRM data for visits and outcomes. Keep platform, date, prompt, country, and page version with each observation. A citation count is a visibility signal, not proof of accuracy, traffic, or commercial value. This is a buyer-side measurement protocol, not a ranking recipe. The source page that prompted the guide is the group’s Dutch-market guide to making pages citable in AI search . This article adds a 16-case evidence ledger for separating Search Console impressions from observed citations and verified support. It helps a team decide what to change, what to leave alone, and what evidence is still missing. The GSC clue is intentionally treated as weak. In a targeted 28-day Search Console pull for this page, 18 October through 13 November 2026, the only page-query row in average positions 8–30 with an impression was “jaap snoeck henkemans seo”: one impression, zero clicks, average position 21. It is a branded query, not a clear non-brand question about AI Search. It does not show that the page earned an AI citation, that a visitor wanted this guide, or that the topic has meaningful demand. We use the page context to choose a decision problem and report the query as a limitation rather than inflate it into market evidence. The practical measurement answer Use this four-row outcome model before discussing “AI visibility” with a client or leadership team: Outcome Evidence What it does not prove Eligibility A canonical page is crawlable, indexed, and can appear with a normal search snippet That a system retrieved it for a prompt Exposure A platform report or reproducible observation shows the page in a generative answer That a person noticed or trusted it Citation and support The answer links to the exact page and a reviewer confirms the passage supports the attached claim That the answer is correct overall or that the link generated a visit Outcome Analytics or CRM evidence connects a visit or action to a source channel and page That a citation caused the action or that every assistant is measured Google’s documentation says generative AI features in Google Search use standard Search eligibility: a page must be indexed and eligible to appear with a snippet. Google also says Search best practices remain relevant; it does not require a special “AI citation” markup or promise inclusion. Fix discoverability and useful content first. Treat an AI citation as an observable result, not a guaranteed output of a checklist. Google’s AI features guidance . Google Search Console documents a dedicated generative AI performance report for Search. Its help page says the report includes impressions for AI Overviews and AI Mode and groups data by page, country, date, and device. That is useful for page-level exposure trends; it is not a prompt-by-prompt citation transcript. Google says the worldwide rollout completed on 31 August 2026, though a property may not show the report if it has not received enough impressions. Google’s report help page and Google’s rollout announcement . That boundary answers a common operator question: “Why can I see impressions but not which exact prompt caused them?” The tool has a defined reporting surface, narrower than a manual prompt experiment. Do not infer an exact prompt from a page-level impression, reverse-engineer a user’s question from a country total, or label Search Console impressions as clicks. For page, country, date, and device trends, use the report. For answer wording and exact source attribution, preserve separate observations. Why one “AI visibility” number misleads An internal report often blends “mentioned,” “cited,” “ranked,” “visited,” and “converted” into one score. These are different events: Mention: a brand or site name appears as text, possibly without a link. Citation: the answer provides a link or source card. Source match: the link resolves to the page you intended to measure after redirects and canonical handling. Support: the cited passage actually supports the claim beside the link. Referral: a user follows a link and lands on your site. Qualified outcome: that visit produces an action that matters to the business. A brand mention with no link may help recall, but it is not a referral path. A citation to a homepage is not a citation to the detailed page you hoped would answer the question. A citation to an exact URL can still be weak evidence if the page does not support the answer. A visitor from an assistant can arrive without a measurable referrer, and a tracked visit may not represent all influence. Name each event before choosing a KPI. Use a stage model rather than a composite score: flowchart LR A[Eligible canonical page] --> B[Retrieved or selected] B --> C[Shown in answer] C --> D[Exact URL cited] D --> E[Passage supports claim] E --> F[Referral visit] F --> G[Qualified outcome] H[Search Console impressions] -. reports exposure .-> C I[Manual prompt log] -. observes .-> B I -. records .-> D J[Analytics and CRM] -. measures where available .-> F J -. measures where available .-> G The diagram is a measurement model, not a claim that every platform exposes every stage. Retrieval may be hidden. Search Console exposes particular impressions and dimensions. Manual observations are a sample of the prompts and dates tested. Analytics records the visits it can attribute. The funnel has blind spots; an honest dashboard labels them instead of filling them with estimates. What the visible results already cover Search results for AI citation tracking now surface three common approaches: official Google Search documentation and Search Console guidance; software-company studies that analyze large result sets or sampled prompts; and practitioner guides recommending prompt lists, recurring checks, and referral analytics. The baseline is familiar: create useful pages, make them available to Search, track citations, and compare visibility over time. Repeating those tips alone does not help a team decide whether an observed citation is meaningful. Google’s documentation is a useful corrective to claims that a publisher must add a special file, schema type, or “AI answer” markup to qualify. It ties generative Search eligibility to ordinary indexing and snippet eligibility and says existing Search practices remain relevant. That is a statement about Google Search, not every third-party assistant. Commercial studies add useful observations but have different scopes. Ahrefs’ March 2026 analysis used 863,000 keyword SERPs and about four million AI Overview URLs from its Brand Radar dataset. It reports that 37.9% of cited URLs also appeared within the first ten result-page blocks when those blocks included regular results and SERP features; 31.2% appeared in blocks 11–100 and 31.0% beyond the first 100 blocks. In a separate organic-blue-links view, 37.1% of cited URLs were in the top ten. The study suggests citations are not limited to top organic ranks, but it does not establish a causal recipe or guarantee that an individual page will be cited. It is one vendor’s crawl and parser, for a particular time and tracked-query set. Ahrefs’ study and methodology . This evidence challenges two overconfident claims. “Only page-one rankings can be cited” is too strong for that dataset. “Ranking no longer matters” is also too strong: a substantial share of cited pages appeared near the top, and the study does not identify a universal mechanism. The sensible inference is narrower: traditional results and AI citations overlap, but they are not identical. That supports separate measurement; it does not support neglecting ordinary Search or promising citations from a new technique. The visible results also contain measurement tools sold by vendors whose products track visibility. Those tools can be useful, but their metric definitions, platform coverage, sampling schedule, and prompt set should be inspectable before a company adopts a KPI. Ask whether “share” is calculated over the same prompts, whether answers were observed at the same time, whether citations mean any link or a specific page, and how missing responses are handled. A chart without definitions may look precise while comparing unlike observations. The missing asset: a citation evidence ledger This ledger records the minimum evidence needed to evaluate an AI Search visibility claim. It is designed for a small SEO, editorial, or analytics team. It is not a measured dataset, platform ranking, representative survey, or API integration. The 16 cases below are test scenarios to apply to your own site. The count is a design choice, not a performance statistic. For each observation, store: run identifier; date and time with timezone; platform and product surface; country and language; exact prompt; signed-in or personalized state if known; page canonical before the run; answer text or a permitted short excerpt; cited URL; final URL after redirects; whether the brand is only mentioned; whether the citation points to the expected canonical page; the claim being supported; the passage that supports it; screenshot or export location; reviewer; and status. If you cannot inspect or retain the answer under the platform’s terms, record “not retained” rather than inventing a transcript. Use a fixed status vocabulary: Status Meaning not-run The prompt has not been tested in this cycle no-answer The platform returned no answer that can be evaluated no-mention No brand or site mention was observed mention-only A name appeared without a clickable source citation-unverified A source link appeared but its destination or support was not checked citation-verified Destination and passage were checked against the stated claim referral-observed A site visit was recorded with the available attribution outcome-observed A defined business action was recorded, with its attribution limits Do not convert “no-answer” into a zero citation rate without defining whether the platform failed, declined, or returned a response with no sources. Do not treat “citation-unverified” as “citation-verified.” The statuses preserve uncertainty that a binary column would erase.
